question: What exactly is a nerve pathway?

options.A: An open space where hormones travel through the bloodstream
options.B: A blood vessel supplying oxygen directly to the brain cells
options.C: The protective fatty covering surrounding peripheral nerve fibers
options.D: The specific route electrical and chemical impulses travel through the nervous system

explanation: Think of a nerve pathway like a designated highway for your body's electrical signals, guiding messages smoothly from where they start to where they need to go! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h1)

question: Why do single neurons connect with hundreds of other neurons instead of working totally alone?

options.A: To prevent the spread of harmful electrical storms in the spinal cord
options.B: To ensure that sensory messages never reach the motor cortex
options.C: To slow down electrical signals so the brain can rest between tasks
options.D: To allow the body to process simple reflexes and complex thoughts simultaneously

explanation: Neurons love teamwork! By linking up in networks, they help your brain multitask effortlessly—handling quick reflexes and deep thoughts all at once. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h1)

question: What do we call bundles of nerve fibers found entirely inside the central nervous system?
explanation: Great to know for exams: inside the brain and spinal cord, fiber bundles are called tracts. Outside the central nervous system, we call them nerves! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h2)

question: Where are ganglia located in the human body?

options.A: Within the center of the spinal cord

explanation: You can picture ganglia as little relay stations located out in the peripheral nervous system, away from the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h2)

question: The spinothalamic tract is famous for carrying which type of sensory information to the brain?
explanation: Whenever you touch something hot or feel a sharp pinch, the spinothalamic tract is the main highway rushing that pain and temperature info up to your brain! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h3)

question: What is the main job of a second-order neuron in a sensory pathway?

options.A: Carrying the signal from the spinal cord or brainstem up to the thalamus
options.B: Detecting the initial environmental stimulus at the skin receptor
options.C: Sending final motor output directly to the skeletal muscle
options.D: Producing neurotransmitters inside the primary motor cortex

explanation: Think of second-order neurons as the middle relay runners, taking the sensory baton from the spinal cord and passing it all the way up to the thalamus. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h3)

question: Which pathway serves as the main route for conscious, precise voluntary movements?
explanation: When you decide to write notes or pick up a pen, the corticospinal tract is the master pathway carrying those commands straight from your brain to your muscles. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h4)

question: A patient with damage only to their lower motor neurons will most likely show which clinical sign?

options.A: Loss of pain and temperature sensation on one side
options.D: Complete inability to process sensory information

explanation: Lower motor neurons connect directly to muscles. When they are damaged, the muscle loses its tone completely, leading to floppiness (flaccidity) and shrinkage (wasting). [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of a reflex arc?

options.A: To allow the cerebral cortex to consciously plan complex body movements
options.B: To transmit deep thought processes from the frontal lobe to organs
options.C: To control an involuntary, rapid response to protect the body from harm
options.D: To store long-term memories in the peripheral nervous system

explanation: Reflexes are your body's built-in safety system! They trigger super-fast, automatic reactions—like pulling your hand away from a hot stove—before you even have time to think. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h5)

question: In a reflex arc, which part carries the nerve impulse away from the central nervous system?
explanation: Motor neurons act like the delivery team, carrying the processed action signal away from the spinal cord out to the muscles or glands to take action. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h5)

question: What do we call the chemical messengers that cross the synaptic cleft?
explanation: Neurotransmitters are the chemical bridge-builders that help a message jump across the tiny gap (synapse) from one neuron to the next. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h6)

question: Why is signal integration at a synapse so important?

options.A: To destroy leftover cellular debris in the extracellular space
options.B: To combine excitatory and inhibitory inputs so the body responds appropriately
options.C: To speed up blood circulation inside the central nervous system
options.D: To permanently convert electrical impulses into physical muscle tissue

explanation: Think of integration like a decision-making meeting. The synapse weighs all the 'go' and 'stop' signals to decide whether the next neuron should fire. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h6)

question: A patient with diabetes mellitus develops peripheral neuropathy. Which symptom would you most expect to see?

options.A: Instant spastic paralysis of both upper extremities
options.B: Rapid increase in cognitive processing speed
options.C: Loss of voluntary control over heart contractions
options.D: Numbness and loss of protective sensation in the feet

explanation: Peripheral neuropathy frequently robs patients of sensation in their hands and feet, which is why daily foot checks are so crucial in nursing care for diabetics! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h7)

question: A stroke damages the motor tracts on the right side of a patient's brain. Where will they likely show physical weakness?

options.B: Only in the facial muscles on the right side
options.C: Equally on both sides of the entire body
options.D: On the left side of the body

explanation: Because our motor pathways cross over to the opposite side, brain damage on the right side causes weakness on the left side of the body. Classic nursing neurology! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T16#GNS211_U3_T16_h7)
